html:
From about 1400 to 1800 the ports of India sat at the centre of a vast trading world that stretched from East Africa and Arabia to China. The historian Fernand Braudel called this Far East, taken together, the greatest world economy of all.

India's strength was cloth. Weavers in Gujarat, on the Coromandel coast and in Bengal made cotton textiles that sold in every port of the ocean. Merchants carried them out and brought back spices, gold, silver, horses and porcelain. The main hubs were:

  • Cambay and later Surat in Gujarat, facing the Red Sea and the Gulf.
  • Calicut on the Malabar coast, the pepper port.
  • The Coromandel ports, trading east to Malacca and the islands.

Indian traders, Hindu, Jain and Muslim, financed much of it. A merchant like Virji Vora of Surat could corner whole markets. When Europeans arrived after Vasco da Gama in 1498, they joined this system rather than replacing it, at first. Only after 1750, as the East India Company took power and Indian calicoes met British machine cloth, did the balance turn.
